title: Max Junestrand and Ilona Loginova: How Cleary Gottlieb & Legora Are Redefining Legal Work
author: Max Junestrand · Ilona Logvinova

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not endorse the cluster’s central claim that automating junior work threatens expertise reproduction. It instead frames automation as beneficial augmentation and addresses competence through continuing supervisory oversight, training, upskilling and workflow evaluation, without proposing reconstructed apprenticeship, simulation or protected independent practice.
qs: And as you look to what kind of the future lawyers work will look like, I think that is a very collaborative space between both human intelligence and machine intelligence and freeing up what a lot of this sort of mundane, repetitive, low level tasks are so that you can do more fun things with the time you have.

And so we will have to just constantly be exercising that supervisory oversight and we are trying to embed that as a practice as much as we can across the organization through learning and training and upskilling.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports process-level AI transformation and continued human expertise, but it does not address whether automating junior work weakens apprenticeship, associate development or partner succession. Its claims about component-task automation, richer advice, investment and pricing therefore do not establish a position on the cluster’s central expertise-pipeline proposition.

And then the human expertise can be that much better, that human expertise layer.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Junestrand discusses future-oriented agent architecture, lawyer-led product development and adoption within law firms. The source does not address whether in-house AI capability strengthens corporate buyers, enables selective insourcing or changes reliance on outside counsel, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source reports Legora’s recruitment of lawyers into legal technology and expresses general enthusiasm for the sector, but it does not address whether AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation or human control. st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source accepts agentic delegation while concretely developing the cluster’s supervision and professional-role themes: AI should remain a copilot under continuing lawyer oversight, with lawyers potentially supervising multiple digital agents. st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source accepts selective, strategically guided adaptation rather than indiscriminate AI adoption and materially extends the cluster with a process-led method: identify workflow steps offering the greatest uplift, defer low-impact uses, and redesign work around maturing capabilities. Its claims remain strategic and prospective rather than supported by measured outcomes.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational implementation rather than access alone, and materially develops the proposition through controlled task-level ROI measurement, process mapping and selective deployment where AI offers the greatest uplift. It also supports a copilot model—automating bounded components rather than complex matters end to end—and links workflow efficiency to fixed-fee margins. Its broader demand and acceleration claims remain forecasts rather than measured sector-wide effects.

kp.k: Partnership embeds AI into collaborative legal work
kp.d: The hosts report that Cleary announced its strategic partnership with Legora on May 1, 2025, following a successful 2024 pilot, with firmwide integration as its aim. Junestrand describes a general assistant, scaled tabular contract review and a Microsoft Word plugin, designed for collaboration among lawyers, clients and machines. Logvinova frames the partnership as embedding machine capabilities directly into legal practice, rather than keeping technology separate from lawyers’ work.
qs: We built a general assistant that ties into a lot of different capabilities. We built a large sort of tabular review, scaled contract review system, and then also a plugin into Microsoft Word.
What we mean by collaborative is not only sort of collaborating between lawyers in the same team, but also with clients
We want to merge machine capabilities and emerging technologies into the practice of law, directly embedding it into the way that lawyers work.

kp.k: Internal data science complements external technology partnerships
kp.d: Logvinova describes a two-pronged strategy: partnering with technology providers while developing internal data science capabilities through Springbok. These capabilities support matter-specific development and joint work with vendors. She recommends selecting partners for their trajectory and roadmap, likening the approach to venture-capital selection rather than a purchase based solely on current functionality.
qs: We understood that we needed to have our own data science capabilities internally.
We are now merging those two prongs of our strategy.
We’re investing in the journey and the roadmap and the opportunity
you want to pick the startups with the highest growth, not necessarily the highest point today.

kp.d: Logvinova presents Cleary X’s founding several years earlier as evidence of leadership’s willingness to experiment with alternative legal service delivery. She describes it as an organically developed ALSP within the firm but operating independently, intended to explore disruption internally rather than encounter it only through external competitors. Her comparison with consulting and financial services supplies a historical analogy for embedding technology in legal work, not measured evidence of equivalent outcomes.
qs: ALSPs are emerging in the industry as disruptors.
we ourselves can have an organically developed ALSP that is part of our firm.
discover that version of disruption internally rather than experiencing it externally.
we’ve seen this across consulting and across financial services

kp.d: Both guests identify disconnected systems as an obstacle to effective deployment. Logvinova treats interoperability as a strategic and technical priority as new capabilities proliferate. In his closing forecast, Junestrand predicts consolidation of user interfaces, not necessarily businesses: agents would connect to multiple underlying applications and deliver more end-to-end work through fewer interfaces.
qs: legal tech historically has suffered from a lot of silos where systems weren’t as interconnected
It is so important to figure out how it all works together.
consolidation, maybe not in businesses, but in UIs.
you will leverage agents and LLMs and software to go into these other pieces of software, connecting to them and deliver a more end-to-end piece of work.

kp.k: Lawyers become supervisors of hybrid teams
kp.d: Logvinova explicitly advocates augmentation rather than replacement. She analogizes overseeing AI to supervising junior associates and predicts that everyone could supervise digital agents within mixed human–digital teams. Cleary is seeking to embed this oversight through learning, training and upskilling. This is a governance position and future role thesis, not evidence of changes in associate numbers or staffing leverage.
qs: It should be a copilot It should never be a replacement
We should always be exercising proper oversight and especially as we get into the realm of agents.
everyone will, can and should be a supervisor to a series of digital agents
we are trying to embed that as a practice as much as we can across the organization through learning and training and upskilling.

kp.d: Junestrand reports building evaluation datasets using historical deal inputs and manually produced outputs, then comparing Legora outputs with those earlier results using human and LLM judges. He says repeated tests can reveal patterns in accuracy, precision and recall and increase confidence before live deployment. He calls for closer collaboration with firms to avoid reliance on irrelevant open datasets; no actual scores, dataset sizes or measured results are supplied.

you can use both a human and an LLM as a judge to score how good the AI generated output is versus the traditionally made output.
you can run that test hundreds of times on each use case
What you don’t want to have is teams like us relying on open data sets that doesn’t have anything to do with the real work that elite law firms are delivering.

kp.k: Agentic workflows plan tasks and request human help
kp.d: Junestrand contrasts Legora’s workflows with fixed conditional automation. He describes sequential natural-language instructions that an agent decomposes through planning and execution layers, using tools and optionally asking a human for guidance. His example combines document review, term extraction, risk analysis against historical company data and report writing. Overnight execution replacing late-night data-room processing is presented as an imaginable future use, not an observed outcome.
qs: the LLM or the agent has access to a planning layer and an execution layer.
you have an LLM that’s calling on a bunch of tools in the correct order.
you can even give this agent access to a tool that’s called ask the human for help
You could totally imagine a world where instead of sitting up till 3 a.m., sort of crunching the last data room findings, you just kick off a couple of these workflows when you go to bed

kp.k: Product architecture bets on future model improvements
kp.d: Junestrand says additional funding enables broader ambitions and feature development, while acknowledging that Legora’s workflow architecture does not maximize performance with current models. He argues it is designed to benefit from subsequent model releases and expanded tool access. He describes iterative co-design with Cleary lawyers, including early prototypes and feedback, as central to identifying legal requirements his technical background does not supply.
qs: the way we built workflows is not the local maximum of today.
If you want to maximize the performance today, would actually build it in a different way
as soon as a new model comes out, it actually drastically improves everything we have.
as soon as we give them something, they ask for more and they push us to ship, develop and keep that really high velocity.

She attributes easy adoption to accessible, attractive design and early success that builds trust despite initial AI trepidation. Both guests report strong uptake; Junestrand recalls an onboarding call exceeding a roughly thousand-person Zoom cap. These are participant accounts rather than independently measured adoption findings.

kp.k: Client value includes broader analysis, not just speed
kp.d: Responding to the host’s question about incentives when work takes less time, Logvinova argues that AI’s value lies in expanding the data and precedents informing human judgment. Her illustrative comparison contrasts manually reviewing four, 10 or 15 precedents with reviewing a hundred or a thousand. She qualifies an initial description of AI as infinite by acknowledging context-window and processing constraints. She predicts faster work across the board and invokes earlier technology-driven increases in work, rather than demonstrating that AI has already increased legal demand.
qs: It’s not infinite, but there is a much broader spectrum
If you’re analyzing the last four, 10, 15 precedents in a manual way
a thousand precedents, a hundred precedents
we are moving faster in a sense by embedding AI, but we are also enabling a broader spectrum for analysis
the work has not decreased. The work has increased.

kp.k: Automate high-impact tasks before entire complex matters
kp.d: Junestrand predicts that AI will perform whatever work it becomes capable of doing, with complexity increasing over time. He distinguishes simple tasks within larger deliveries from complete antitrust matters and argues that elite firms are well positioned to benefit. His practical recommendation is to analyze processes and deploy AI where its contribution is largest, deferring low-impact use cases.
qs: every piece of work that AI can do, it will do.
AI is not coming for the, for the sort of full end to end antitrust matter, but it’s coming for simple work or pieces of tasks within a broader ecosystem of a delivery.
where in the process does AI have the biggest uplift? Let’s go deploy it there.

kp.k: AI-native infrastructure and immersive collaboration remain forecasts
kp.d: Logvinova predicts that AI will move from application front ends into core infrastructure. She also speculates that goggles and immersive digital environments could reshape international collaboration, conference rooms and legal workspaces, suggesting an uncertain horizon of 18 months, two years or less. The discussion does not establish that Cleary has implemented such environments or committed to conducting transactions through them.
qs: AI will start to move from the front end of applications of programs of tools, right? To the back end infrastructure as being a core driver and engine of those tools.
we’ll all be wearing goggles in that room and interacting with people across the world.
it’s actually maybe like 18 months away or two years away or even less than that.
we’ll have to see.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Junestrand and Logvinova describe AI as a means of automating routine tasks, expanding legal analysis and collaboration, and moving lawyers toward supervision of hybrid human–agent teams. They also predict changes in competition, pricing incentives and legal-technology interfaces.
pts.d: Junestrand (03:49, 08:13) argues that human–machine collaboration frees lawyers from mundane work and that firms can differentiate themselves through how they deploy and connect otherwise similar technologies. Logvinova (06:10) describes Cleary's combination of external technology partnerships and internal Springbok data-science capabilities as enabling more tailored development. At 18:40, she advocates augmentation rather than replacement and predicts that everyone will supervise digital agents alongside human workers. Junestrand (22:41) describes workflows in which an LLM plans and executes multistep tasks using tools, with the ability to ask a human for help; he imagines lawyers initiating workflows overnight rather than personally completing late-night data-room work. At 29:33, he reports increasing fixed-fee and budget-based arrangements and argues that efficiency increases firms' margins under those arrangements. Logvinova (37:38) argues that AI's value is not merely speed: reviewing a larger body of precedents can improve the human expertise applied to client advice. She predicts faster work and analytics over the next few years, invoking earlier technologies whose introduction did not reduce the amount of legal work. Junestrand (39:59) predicts that AI will perform whatever work it can, initially targeting simpler tasks within complex matters rather than entire sophisticated engagements. At 41:32, he predicts consolidation of user interfaces, not necessarily businesses, as agents connect separate tools. Logvinova (42:28) predicts AI becoming core back-end infrastructure and speculates about immersive, goggles-based collaboration and workspaces.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers primarily offer firsthand implementation experience, product descriptions, evaluation methods and illustrative examples; the transcript does not report quantified productivity, accuracy, profitability or client-outcome results.
pts.d: Junestrand's and Logvinova's accounts draw on their respective roles as Legora's founder and Cleary's practice-innovation director. Junestrand (14:36) recalls an onboarding call reaching a roughly thousand-person Zoom capacity, while Logvinova (28:11, 33:06) reports organic adoption, early pilot success and ongoing usage analytics. These support their descriptions of interest and uptake, rather than establishing measured client benefits. Junestrand (20:11) describes evaluating workflows against historical deals: compare AI output with previously human-created output, use human and LLM judges, and repeat tests to examine accuracy, precision and recall. He gives no resulting scores, sample sizes or independent validation. This is workflow evaluation, distinct from the continuing human oversight Logvinova prescribes for live work. Junestrand (29:33) says individual-task time, turnaround and quality improvements can be calculated but acknowledges the difficulty of firm-wide measurement. His fixed-fee trend claim is an experiential observation without supporting market data; the $300 million budget is an illustrative formulation, not an identified transaction. Logvinova's broader-analysis claim uses hypothetical comparisons between manually reviewing a few precedents and AI-assisted review of hundreds or thousands. Her expectations about work volume draw on historical analogy with earlier communications technologies. Her immersive-workspace forecast cites a news report about a screen-free laptop, not an observed legal deployment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account combines current deployment experience in 2025 with conditional forecasts: continuing model improvement, human oversight, usable design, integration and appropriate use-case selection underpin the predicted changes.
pts.d: Logvinova (10:50) locates the improvement that made generative AI compelling for legal work in roughly the previous year, beginning around spring 2024. Junestrand describes agents and MCP as becoming production-ready and presents Legora's workflows as designed for 2025 and future model capabilities rather than for maximum present-day performance. At 25:35, he explicitly concedes that optimizing today's performance would entail a different design, arguing that future models and additional tools will improve the chosen architecture. Logvinova's supervisory-team model is a future-state thesis without a firm date, conditioned on governance, continuing oversight, training and upskilling. Her adoption approach begins with accessible, high-value, broadly applicable use cases before more specialized tools. Her claim about broader data analysis is expressly bounded by context windows and processing limits; she retracts an initial characterization of AI as infinite. Junestrand (39:59) qualifies task automation by present complexity limits and recommends prioritizing processes where AI offers the greatest uplift. His interface-consolidation forecast has no precise deadline, although he says it is moving faster than many expect. Logvinova predicts faster processing and analytics over the next few years and suggests immersive workplace changes could be 18 months to two years away, or sooner. These are forecasts rather than implementation commitments.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are lawyers at large, sophisticated firms, their clients, innovation and technical teams, and legal-technology providers; the discussion does not offer a concrete access-to-justice or profession-wide employment forecast.
pts.d: For lawyers, Junestrand predicts less routine processing and more guidance of AI systems; Logvinova envisages supervisory responsibilities extending across the workforce through hybrid human–digital teams. Her comparison with supervising junior associates describes an oversight model, not a quantified forecast of junior-lawyer displacement. Clients are presented as collaborators and beneficiaries of broader evidence-informed analysis and improved advice. Junestrand argues that elite firms are well positioned because AI can improve components of complex matters without presently handling the entire engagement. Firms face investment requirements and potentially different competitive outcomes depending on implementation; under fixed-fee or budget-based delivery, efficiency can improve margins. Innovation, internal data-science, information-security and risk teams support customization, integration, training and analytics, while vendors work with practitioners to co-design features. Logvinova (10:50) also describes Cleary X as an internally developed ALSP intended to let the firm explore disruption internally rather than encounter it only externally; this is distinct from Legora's role as a software provider. Junestrand's interface forecast affects both lawyers navigating numerous tools and vendors whose products may be accessed through agents rather than directly. At 45:42, he identifies current opportunities for lawyers to move into legal technology through Legora's hiring in New York, London and Stockholm.
